name: Valproate (Divalproex/Valproic Acid) (Depakote)
summary: Mood stabilizer used for acute mania and mixed episodes in bipolar disorder. Can work within days (especially with loading) but carries serious risks—most importantly liver failure, pancreatitis, and major pregnancy-related harms.
description: Valproate (often prescribed as Depakote/divalproex) is a classic bipolar medication for calming acute mania and mixed episodes—especially when symptoms are loud, fast, and hard to contain. It can start helping within a few days, but it’s not a casual med. It can cause serious (rare but real) liver failure, life-threatening pancreatitis, and significant fetal risk. It also commonly causes weight gain, tremor, sedation, and GI upset. This is a medication where labs and safety checks matter.
patient_summary: Valproate (Depakote/divalproex) can calm mania and mixed episodes quickly—sometimes within days. But it’s a high-stakes medication: rare liver failure and pancreatitis can be fatal, and pregnancy exposure can cause major birth defects and long-term neurodevelopmental harm. It can also cause weight gain, tremor, sedation, and stomach side effects. If you’re on it, monitoring and contraception counseling (when relevant) are non-negotiable.

metadata.pharmacologic_category: Valproate (GABA-Enhancing Antiseizure Agent) used as a mood stabilizer in psychiatry

linked_conditions.context: Used for acute mania and mixed episodes. Often chosen when symptoms are severe, sleep is collapsing, irritability is high, or there’s agitation. May be used alone or combined with an antipsychotic depending on episode intensity.
Sometimes continued as maintenance if it clearly prevented relapse for that person. Not everyone is a great fit—side effects and reproductive safety often drive the long-term plan.
Not a go-to for bipolar depression, but sometimes used as an alternative agent (mono- or adjunctive therapy) when other options haven’t worked or aren’t tolerated.
May be used in select cases to help stabilize agitation when it’s tied to mood cycling (especially mixed features). Not recommended for dementia-related agitation due to poor benefit and higher harm.

contraindications: Hepatic disease or significant hepatic impairment
Known mitochondrial disorders caused by POLG mutations (eg, Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome)
Children <2 years of age who are clinically suspected of a mitochondrial disorder
Pregnancy: avoid for bipolar disorder unless other medications have failed or are unacceptable (high fetal risk)
Hypersensitivity to valproate/divalproex/derivatives or formulation components

efficacy_response.metric: Time to noticeable calming of mania
efficacy_response.patient_text: For acute mania or mixed episodes, valproate can start taking the edge off within a few days—especially if your prescriber uses a loading strategy—while full stabilization may take 1 to 2 weeks. The goal is fewer racing thoughts, less impulsive energy, less irritability, and sleep that stops falling apart.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Well absorbed; food may delay absorption but does not meaningfully reduce overall absorption
pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: Extended-release is ~90% relative to IV and slightly lower than delayed-release
pharmacokinetics.onset: Varies by target symptom; calming of mania may begin within days
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Adults: ~9 to 19 hours (longer in neonates, older adults, and hepatic impairment)
pharmacokinetics.duration_IR: Depends on dosing schedule; often divided dosing for stable levels
pharmacokinetics.duration_XR: Smoother daily profile with less fluctuation; commonly once daily
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensively hepatic (glucuronidation and mitochondrial beta-oxidation; additional oxidative pathways)
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Urine primarily as metabolites; minimal unchanged drug
pharmacokinetics.protein_binding: High and concentration-dependent (typically 80% to 90%); free fraction increases with hypoalbuminemia, kidney impairment, and higher levels
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: May help GI tolerability; may delay peak levels

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Valproate (often prescribed as Depakote/divalproex) is used in psychiatry mainly for stabilizing {link:condition:bipolar-i-disorder:bipolar I disorder} when someone is in acute mania or a mixed episode. It’s a strong option when symptoms are intense—fast speech, impulsivity, agitation, reduced need for sleep, irritability—and you need the episode to come down safely.
items: {link:condition:bipolar-i-disorder:Acute mania}: Elevated/irritable mood, risky behavior, racing thoughts, decreased need for sleep
Mixed episodes: Manic energy with depression/anxiety features (often the most uncomfortable and high-risk state)
Adjunctive use: Sometimes combined with an antipsychotic when symptoms are severe, psychosis is present, or agitation is escalating
Maintenance (select cases): Continued if it clearly prevents relapse and side effects are acceptable
off_label: Mood-related agitation (carefully selected cases, not dementia-related agitation)
Irritability and impulsive aggression when clearly tied to mood cycling (case-by-case, specialist-guided)

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Valproate can feel like a “turning down” medication—helpful for mania, but sometimes a little too sedating or heavy. Here’s how people commonly describe it:

quotes: It didn’t erase my personality—it just stopped my brain from running at 200 miles an hour.
I finally slept. That’s when I knew it was starting to work.
The irritability backed off. I wasn’t snapping at everyone all day.
It calmed me, but I also felt kind of sleepy and flat at first.
My thoughts were quieter—but I was a little foggy for a while.
It helped me stop spiraling, but mornings felt heavy.
items.note: Sedation is common early on and with dose increases. It often improves, but if it doesn’t, your dose or schedule may need adjusting.

quotes: I had nausea at the beginning—taking it with food helped.
My appetite went up and I had to watch my weight.
Once my body adjusted, the GI stuff got better.

items.category: Tremor, Hair Changes, and ‘Body’ Side Effects
quotes: My hands shook a bit, especially if the dose was higher.
My hair felt thinner for a while, which freaked me out.
The trade-off was real: mood better, body side effects annoying.
This is not a ‘set it and forget it’ med. The labs are part of the deal.
I felt fine—but my doctor still checked levels and liver tests.
It worked, but the pregnancy warning was a huge conversation.
items.note: Monitoring is not optional with valproate—especially early in treatment and in anyone who could become pregnant.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Valproate isn’t instant like a sedative, but it can move faster than many long-term mood medications—especially for acute mania.
key_points: First few days: Some people notice improved sleep and reduced agitation (especially with loading strategies)
1 week: Clearer reduction in manic intensity for many patients
1-2 weeks: More complete stabilization becomes more likely as dose/level is optimized
Half-life (adults): ~9-19 hours (longer in older adults and liver impairment)
Extended-release (ER): Smoother daily levels with less fluctuation than delayed-release (DR)

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Valproate is widely used for acute mania and mixed episodes because it can bring intensity down relatively quickly and can be combined with an antipsychotic when symptoms are severe. The practical target is fewer racing thoughts, less impulsivity, less agitation, and sleep that returns.
sections.clinical_details: Response is strongly dose- and level-dependent. Many clinicians aim for therapeutic serum concentrations while tracking real-life function: sleep, pacing/speech pressure, irritability, spending/sexual impulsivity, goal-directed overactivity, and safety risks. Some people respond dramatically; others feel mainly side effects. If there’s no meaningful change after dose optimization and time, the plan should shift.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Valproate can cause fatal liver failure and life-threatening pancreatitis—and it carries major pregnancy-related risks.
sections.black_box: Serious or fatal hepatotoxicity has occurred, usually within the first 6 months. Life-threatening pancreatitis has been reported in children and adults. In pregnancy, valproate can cause major congenital malformations (including neural tube defects) and long-term neurodevelopmental harm (including lower IQ and increased neurodevelopmental disorders).
other: Hepatotoxicity risk is highest early (first 6 months) and higher in very young children, mitochondrial disease, metabolic disorders, and polytherapy
Contraindicated in known POLG-related mitochondrial disorders; avoid in children <2 years suspected of mitochondrial disease
Pancreatitis can occur shortly after starting or after years; can progress rapidly and be fatal
Hyperammonemia and encephalopathy can occur with or without liver failure (can look like sudden confusion, lethargy, vomiting)
Hematologic toxicity can occur (thrombocytopenia, impaired platelet function, bleeding risk)
Suicidal thoughts/behavior warning applies to antiseizure medications as a class
Not recommended for dementia-related agitation or aggression (poor benefit, higher adverse effects)
patient_counseling: If you develop severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or loss of appetite—treat it as urgent. Pancreatitis is rare but dangerous.
In the first 6 months, watch for vague ‘flu-like’ danger signs: malaise, weakness, sleepiness, facial swelling, poor appetite, vomiting. That can be early liver toxicity—don’t ignore it.
If you could become pregnant, this medication requires a serious contraception and pregnancy-risk conversation. This is not a casual warning.
Don’t stop suddenly unless your prescriber tells you to—stopping abruptly can destabilize mood, and in people with seizure risk it can be dangerous.
Report unusual bruising, bleeding, or extreme fatigue—those can be blood-related side effects.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common: GI upset (nausea, vomiting), sedation/drowsiness, tremor, weight gain, and hair thinning. Serious but rare: liver failure, pancreatitis, hyperammonemic encephalopathy, and severe blood or skin reactions.
plain_language_list: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain (often improves with food or slow titration)
Low platelets and easier bruising/bleeding (dose/level-related for many patients)
Confusion/lethargy from high ammonia (can happen even if liver tests look okay)

common.incidence: >10% reported in labeling (varies by symptom and formulation)
common.patient_note: Taking it with food and increasing the dose slowly can make a big difference. If you can’t keep food down or symptoms are severe, your prescriber should know—sometimes the formulation or schedule needs to change.
Early sedation is common. If it’s crushing your daytime function, dosing time or the total dose may need adjusting. Older adults are more sensitive and usually need lower doses.
Tremor is often dose- or level-related. Sometimes lowering the dose slightly fixes it without losing mood stability.
This is one of the most common reasons people stop valproate. Tracking weight early (not months later) helps you catch changes before they snowball.
Hair changes can happen and are often reversible. It’s upsetting, and it’s real—bring it up early so your prescriber can weigh options.
Some people feel calmer but also a bit dulled. The goal is stability without losing your brain. If you feel ‘too slowed down,’ dosing and alternatives should be discussed.

serious: Hepatotoxicity and hepatic failure (can be fatal): watch for malaise, weakness, lethargy, facial edema, loss of appetite, vomiting, jaundice; highest risk early (first 6 months).
Pancreatitis (can be hemorrhagic and rapidly fatal): severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, anorexia—requires urgent evaluation and usually discontinuation.
Hyperammonemia / hyperammonemic encephalopathy: drowsiness, vomiting, confusion, slowed thinking, decreased consciousness, focal neurologic symptoms—check ammonia and reassess therapy.
Coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia: bruising, bleeding, hemorrhage risk; rare severe complications reported.
Severe cutaneous reactions (SJS/TEN/DRESS): rash with fever, mucosal sores, facial swelling, swollen lymph nodes, organ symptoms—medical emergency.
Reproductive/endocrine effects: menstrual irregularities, polycystic ovary syndrome features, hyperandrogenism; fertility-related changes have been reported in all sexes.
Suicidal ideation/behavior: class warning for antiseizure medications; monitor mood and safety closely.

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Valproate has interaction landmines. Some raise side effects (like sedation, bleeding, ammonia issues). Others can drastically change levels—meaning your dose that ‘worked’ suddenly doesn’t.

items.risk: Valproate can increase lamotrigine levels and raise the risk of serious rash (including SJS/TEN) if lamotrigine is titrated too fast.
items.action: If combined, lamotrigine must be started at a lower dose and increased more slowly than usual. Any rash needs urgent evaluation.

items.risk: Increased risk of hyperammonemia and encephalopathy—even if either medication was previously tolerated alone.
items.action: Use caution, monitor for confusion/lethargy/vomiting, and check ammonia if symptoms appear.

items.risk: Additive CNS depression (more sedation, impaired judgment, falls).
items.action: Avoid or minimize alcohol; be cautious with sleep aids, antihistamines, and other sedating meds.

items.with: Aspirin and other highly protein-bound drugs
items.risk: Can increase the free (active) fraction of valproate, raising toxicity risk even if total level looks “fine.”
items.action: If symptoms suggest toxicity, consider checking free valproate level and reassessing the med combo.

items.risk: Bleeding risk can increase due to platelet effects and potential coagulation changes.
items.action: Monitor closely for bruising/bleeding and coordinate labs when clinically indicated.

items.risk: Can alter valproate levels and increase adverse effects; complex bidirectional interactions are possible.
items.action: Specialist-guided dosing and monitoring is recommended when combining.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Valproate shouldn’t be stopped abruptly unless there’s a safety emergency (like suspected pancreatitis or severe liver injury). In bipolar disorder, stopping too fast increases the risk of mood relapse—especially mania/hypomania returning hard.
key_points: Typical approach (bipolar): Gradual taper over weeks, with close monitoring for early return of mania/hypomania (sleep reduction, irritability, increased goal-directed activity).
If you’ve been stable on valproate for a long time, tapering too quickly can trigger relapse—slow is safer.
Emergency stop situations: suspected pancreatitis, severe hypersensitivity reaction, or suspected severe liver injury usually requires stopping and switching to an alternative plan.
After discontinuation for bipolar disorder: monitor for several weeks to months for reemergence of symptoms.
If there’s any seizure history or seizure risk, tapering needs extra caution and coordination.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Valproate dosing in bipolar disorder is usually adjusted based on symptoms plus serum levels. There are different formulations (immediate, delayed-release, extended-release), and the schedule depends on what you’re taking and what your body tolerates.

adult.mania_initial: 500 to 750 mg/day PO (total daily dose) in 1 to 4 divided doses depending on formulation
adult.mania_titration: Increase by 250 to 500 mg/day every 1 to 3 days to reach clinical effect and a therapeutic serum concentration
adult.mania_typical: Often 1,500 to 2,500 mg/day total (varies by body size, formulation, and tolerability)
adult.loading_option: For rapid control: 20 to 30 mg/kg/day PO in divided doses for 2 to 3 days, then adjust based on response and levels (some experts limit initial loading to 20 mg/kg/day, up to 2,000 mg/day if >100 kg)
adult.maintenance: Continue the dose (and any combination regimen) that achieved control of the acute episode, then re-check tolerability, labs, and long-term risk/benefit

sections.simple_explanation: Think of valproate like a ‘level-based’ mood stabilizer. Your prescriber may start with a standard dose, then adjust every few days based on how you’re doing and what your blood level shows. ER can be smoother for some people; DR/IR may be divided to keep levels steady and reduce side effects.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Valproate has some of the most serious reproductive warnings in psychiatry. It also has specific high-risk groups where it should be avoided or used only with extreme caution.
sections.pregnancy: High fetal risk. Valproate can cause major congenital malformations (including neural tube defects like spina bifida) and is linked to long-term neurodevelopmental harms (including lower IQ and increased risk of neurodevelopmental disorders) after in utero exposure. For bipolar disorder, it should not be used in pregnancy unless other medications have failed or are unacceptable. In patients who could become pregnant, it should not be used unless other options fail or are unacceptable, and effective contraception should be used.
sections.lactation: Valproate enters breast milk at relatively low levels compared with many other antiseizure medications and is often considered compatible with breastfeeding. However, infants should be monitored for signs of liver problems (jaundice), unusual bruising/bleeding, poor feeding, sedation, and appropriate weight gain. If toxicity is suspected, infant serum levels may be checked.
sections.geriatrics: Older adults are more sensitive to sedation and dehydration risk. Lower initial and maintenance doses (often 50% to 60% of usual) are commonly recommended, with close monitoring for somnolence, nutritional intake, and falls.
sections.hepatic: Avoid in significant hepatic impairment. Use is contraindicated in Child-Turcotte-Pugh class B or C. Even mild impairment increases the free (active) fraction due to lower albumin, so total levels can look ‘normal’ while free levels are too high—free level monitoring is preferred when available.
sections.renal: No standard dose adjustment is usually required, but protein binding is reduced in severe kidney impairment, so free valproate may be higher than expected. Total levels can be misleading; monitor clinical response and consider free levels when available.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Liver safety: Baseline liver tests and frequent monitoring during the first 6 months. Watch for early warning symptoms (malaise, weakness, lethargy, facial edema, anorexia, vomiting, jaundice).
Pancreatitis warning signs: Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, anorexia—prompt evaluation is required.
CBC with platelets: Baseline and periodic monitoring for thrombocytopenia and bleeding risk.
Coagulation labs (PT/PTT): Especially if there’s bleeding risk, before procedures, or if clinical concern arises.

Serum valproate concentrations: Use trough levels for interpretation; consider free valproate levels when albumin is low, kidney function is poor, or symptoms suggest toxicity despite ‘normal’ total levels.
Ammonia: Check if unexplained lethargy, vomiting, hypothermia, confusion, slowed cognition, or mental status changes occur (hyperammonemic encephalopathy can occur even without clear liver failure).
Mood and safety: Monitor for depression, agitation changes, and suicidal thoughts/behavior (class warning).
Weight and metabolic tracking: Weight changes can be early; track before it becomes a long-term problem.
Neurologic/cognitive function: Monitor for tremor, parkinsonism-like symptoms, and cognitive slowing—especially in long-term use.
Reproductive/endocrine monitoring: Menstrual history and features of PCOS (especially in the first year), plus counseling on fertility-related effects as relevant.
Pregnancy status and contraception counseling: Evaluate pregnancy status when clinically appropriate and document shared decision-making about risks.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Valproate comes in multiple forms, and the formulation affects dosing schedule and blood level smoothness. ER is often once daily; DR/IR are often divided to reduce fluctuations.
items: Delayed-Release Tablets (divalproex sodium): 125 mg, 250 mg, 500 mg
Extended-Release Tablets (divalproex sodium ER): 250 mg, 500 mg
Delayed-Release Sprinkle Capsules: 125 mg
Immediate-Release Capsules (valproic acid): 250 mg
Oral Solution/Syrup: 250 mg/5 mL (concentration varies by product/region)
IV Solution (valproate sodium): 100 mg/mL

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Valproate reduces brain over-excitation through multiple pathways. In plain language: it helps strengthen inhibitory signaling (GABA—the brain’s “calm” system), and it also affects electrical firing through sodium channels and other excitatory systems. The end result is a steadier, less “revved up” brain state, which is why it can calm mania and mixed episodes.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Valproate is a workhorse medication for acute mania and mixed episodes—especially when symptoms are severe, agitation is present, and sleep is collapsing. It’s often used alongside an antipsychotic for faster stabilization. Long-term use is a risk-benefit decision: some people do great on it, but weight gain, sedation, and the reproductive/pregnancy risks can be deal-breakers. It is generally avoided in people who are pregnant or could become pregnant unless other options have clearly failed and the safety plan is tight.

seo.title: Valproate (Depakote): Uses, Dosing, Side Effects, Labs, and Pregnancy Risks
seo.description: Valproate (Depakote/divalproex) for bipolar mania and mixed episodes: how fast it works, dosing basics, common side effects (weight gain, tremor, sedation), serious warnings (liver failure, pancreatitis, hyperammonemia), key interactions, and required monitoring.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.q: What is valproate (Depakote) used for in psychiatry?
faqs.a: In psychiatry, valproate is mainly used for bipolar disorder—especially acute mania and mixed episodes. It’s often chosen when symptoms are intense (agitation, irritability, risky behavior, racing thoughts, decreased need for sleep) and you need the episode to come down safely.

faqs.q: How fast does Depakote work for mania?
faqs.a: Some people notice improvement within a few days—often starting with sleep improving and agitation easing—especially if a loading strategy is used. More complete stabilization typically takes 1 to 2 weeks as the dose and blood level are optimized.

faqs.q: Do I need bloodwork on valproate?
faqs.a: Yes. Valproate is a lab-monitored medication. Liver tests are checked at baseline and frequently during the first 6 months. Platelets/CBC are monitored for bleeding risk. Serum valproate levels are often checked to guide dosing, and ammonia is checked if symptoms suggest hyperammonemic encephalopathy (sudden confusion, lethargy, vomiting).

faqs.q: What are the biggest danger signs I should not ignore?
faqs.a: Severe abdominal pain with nausea/vomiting or loss of appetite can be pancreatitis—urgent evaluation is needed. Early liver toxicity can start with vague symptoms like malaise, weakness, lethargy, facial swelling, poor appetite, and vomiting. Sudden confusion, extreme sleepiness, or mental status changes can be hyperammonemia. Any of these should be treated as urgent.

Valproate has high fetal risk. It can cause major congenital malformations (including neural tube defects) and is linked to long-term neurodevelopmental harm after in utero exposure. In bipolar disorder, it should not be used in pregnancy unless other options have failed or are unacceptable. If someone could become pregnant, it should not be used unless other options have failed or are unacceptable—and effective contraception should be used.

Yes. Weight gain and increased appetite are common and are among the top reasons people discontinue it. The best move is early tracking (weight, appetite changes) so you catch shifts before they become a long-term problem.

faqs.q: Why do some people feel foggy or sleepy on valproate?
faqs.a: Valproate can cause CNS depression—sleepiness, slowed thinking, and a ‘heavier’ feeling—especially early in treatment or after dose increases. If sedation is interfering with functioning, dosing schedule, formulation (ER vs DR), or the total dose may need adjustment.

faqs.q: What’s the difference between Depakote DR and Depakote ER?
faqs.a: DR (delayed-release) is commonly taken in divided doses to maintain stable levels. ER (extended-release) is designed for a smoother daily profile and is commonly taken once daily. ER is not directly interchangeable with DR at the same dose—dose conversion is sometimes needed to maintain similar serum concentrations.

faqs.q: Can I stop Depakote suddenly if I feel better?
faqs.a: Don’t stop suddenly unless your prescriber tells you to. In bipolar disorder, stopping too fast increases the risk of relapse—especially mania or hypomania coming back. If the medication needs to be stopped for safety reasons (like suspected pancreatitis or severe liver injury), your prescriber will shift you to an alternative plan.

Yes. Valproate can increase lamotrigine exposure and raise the risk of serious rash if lamotrigine is titrated too quickly. When the two are combined, lamotrigine is typically started lower and increased more slowly, and any rash needs urgent evaluation.

faqs.q: Is valproate used for dementia-related agitation?
faqs.a: It’s not recommended for dementia-related agitation or aggression because evidence suggests limited benefit and increased risk of adverse effects. In those situations, clinicians generally look for other approaches.
